title: Beauty In My Backyard - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: The argument that architectural ugliness blocks development not through local NIMBY opposition but through diffuse non-local 'NITBY' sentiment: restrictive zoning predates modernism by a generation, postwar demolition rates were historically normal, and heritage conservation exploded in the 1960s-70s only once modernism made redevelopment read as uglification. The result is frozen European city centers, 'L transect' New World cities, and a heritage constraint concentrated on exactly the most economically valuable land.

insights.claim: Opposition to new development splits into two distinct constituencies: local residents (NIMBYs) motivated mainly by construction disruption, loss of green space, pressure on services and social exclusivity, and non-local objectors (NITBYs) motivated mainly by aesthetics.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Design-led reform pitches beauty at NIMBYs, but the aesthetic constituency that actually blocks central redevelopment lives elsewhere — target campaigns accordingly.
insights.quote: Let us call the second group ‘NITBYs’, for ‘Not in that backyard’.
insights.locator: Local opponents have many other concerns

insights.claim: Most opponents of a development who live nowhere near it are only casually interested and broadly altruistic, judging on a cursory assessment whether a scheme improves its neighborhood — yet their diffuse, low-effort support aggregates into a decisive political force in a democracy.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Diffuse passive preferences, not organized local lobbies, set the ceiling on urban redevelopment — a reason planning liberalization keeps under-delivering in historic cores.
insights.quote: While a few NITBYs are fervent campaigners, most are only casually interested.
insights.locator: While a few NITBYs are fervent campaigners

insights.claim: Beauty is not a reliable purchase of local consent: I’On in Charleston, South Carolina, one of North America’s loveliest neighborhoods, drew petitions from thousands of locals, an initial town council rejection, and a referendum campaign to downzone the site, and survived only because the South Carolina Supreme Court ruled that zoning decisions cannot be made by referendum.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Underwriting a 'beautiful design defeats objections' entitlement strategy is risky — attractive schemes still face multi-year legal and referendum risk.
insights.quote: The NIMBYs were defeated only after the South Carolina Supreme Court found that zoning decisions cannot be made by referendum.
insights.locator: I’On (pronounced ‘ion’) in Charleston

insights.claim: The Duchy of Cornwall’s proposed South East Faversham scheme in Kent — by the same landowner behind Poundbury and Nansledan, and among the most appealing urban extensions in modern Europe — has triggered hundreds of protest letters plus opposition from Faversham Council, neighboring councils and the local MP.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Even royal patronage and a proven traditional-design track record do not clear UK planning risk; land option pricing on 'beautiful' schemes should not assume faster consent.
insights.quote: Nonetheless, it has triggered hundreds of letters of protest, as well as opposition from Faversham Council, the neighboring councils, and the local Member of Parliament.
insights.locator: The Duchy is currently proposing a third

insights.claim: Even the most beautiful finished neighborhood is preceded by several years of extreme ugliness while under construction, so aesthetic quality can never fully neutralize the objections of people who live next to a building site.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Explains why construction-phase mitigation, not architectural style, is what actually moves adjacent-owner opposition.
insights.quote: even the most beautiful neighborhood only emerges after several years of extreme ugliness, while the buildings are under construction
insights.locator: Perhaps this should not surprise us

insights.claim: Restrictive zoning spread across the West a full generation before modernist architecture existed: Germany and Austria-Hungary in the 1890s, Italian cities in the 1900s, a British national framework in 1909, France in 1919 and the United States through the interwar period, whereas modernism emerged in 1920s Germany and only triumphed globally in the 1950s.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Kills the causal story that ugly buildings produced restrictive land-use law — the restrictions came first, so beautification alone will not undo them.
insights.quote: Restrictive zoning emerged in Germany and Austria-Hungary in the 1890s and spread quickly thereafter.
insights.locator: In fact, however, these changes happened in the wrong order

insights.claim: Most German and Austrian suburbs were capped at their existing densities well before 1914 and still retain those densities today, showing that the tightest European density controls were locked in more than a century ago.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Continental European supply constraints are structurally ancient, not a recent policy error — expect very slow reversal and persistent rent pressure.
insights.quote: in Germany and Austria most suburbs were capped at their existing densities well before 1914, and retain those densities today
insights.locator: The restrictiveness of early zoning varied by country

insights.claim: The buildings banned by early twentieth-century zoning were traditional in style — flats with classical cornices, pedimented windows and rusticated basements — meaning the Great Downzoning was imposed on architecture the public liked, not on architecture it found ugly.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Undercuts the beauty-as-policy-unlock thesis for suburban zoning reform; the binding motive there was exclusion, not taste.
insights.quote: The flats that were banned by early zoning would generally have had classical cornices, pedimented windows, and rusticated basements.
insights.locator: This means that the Great Downzoning happened

insights.claim: Because restrictive land-use rules were entrenched before the average new building became uglier than the average old one, making new development beautiful would palliate local opposition only modestly.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations for design codes and 'street votes' style reforms — they are not a general cure for suburban supply constraints.
insights.locator: This suggests that, though making development beautiful

insights.claim: Paris retains only two fully intact timber-framed houses, at 11 and 13 Rue François-Miron, despite never suffering a great fire, earthquake or destructive bombing — its tens of thousands of medieval timber houses were simply demolished for ordinary redevelopment over the centuries.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Historic-preservation absolutism is a modern invention; the baseline for European cities was continuous demolition and replacement.
insights.quote: Until the sixteenth century, almost all houses in Paris were timber-framed.
insights.locator: A graphic illustration of this is visible

insights.claim: Of roughly 100,000 homes in the brick-built London rebuilt after the 1666 Great Fire, only 100 to 200 survive today, a destruction rate of about 99.8 percent — more thorough than the fire itself, and mostly accomplished before modernism through eighteenth, nineteenth and early twentieth-century redevelopment.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: The 'postwar planners destroyed our cities' narrative that justifies conservation law does not survive contact with pre-modern demolition rates.
insights.quote: that means a destruction rate of 99.8 percent, considerably more thorough than that of the Great Fire
insights.locator: Assuming 100,000 homes in 1700

insights.claim: Fewer than twenty pre-1800 buildings of any kind survive in New York and perhaps fifty to a hundred in Boston, with most losses occurring in the nineteenth century and the Roaring Twenties building boom, long before modernism arrived.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: American urban stock has always been treated as depreciating and replaceable — today’s protection regime is the anomaly, not the demolition.
insights.quote: Almost all of these buildings were already gone before the rise of modernism, demolished in the nineteenth century or in the furious building activity of the Roaring Twenties.
insights.locator: This process was perhaps even more marked

insights.claim: Roughly three quarters of Manhattan’s several hundred Gilded Age urban palaces were demolished in a short burst in the late 1920s — the Cornelius Vanderbilt II House in 1926 for Bergdorf Goodman, the Mrs William B Astor House in 1926 for Temple Emanu-El, and the Elbridge T Gerry Mansion in 1929 for the Pierre hotel — and all three replacements now themselves enjoy heritage protection.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Heritage status is a moving, arbitrary designation applied to whatever the last generation built — it is a political variable, not a fixed property of buildings.
insights.quote: Ironically, all three of these buildings now have heritage protection, either as individual landmarks or as elements of historic districts.
insights.locator: In the Gilded Age, Manhattan had several hundred urban palaces

insights.claim: Britain demolished at least 1.5 million homes in postwar slum clearance, roughly 10 percent of the total housing stock but 15 to 20 percent of the prewar stock, while in the United States nearly half of the 12,000 buildings recorded in the 1933 Historic American Buildings Survey had been demolished or seriously mutilated by the mid-1960s.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Quantifies the mid-century clearance wave that conservation law was built to stop — the reference point for how much supply an unconstrained regime can create.
insights.quote: In Britain, the government actually did demolish at least 1.5 million homes in slum clearance schemes in the postwar decades.
insights.locator: In Britain, the government actually did demolish

insights.claim: Conservation policy brought demolition of old stock almost to a standstill: France demolished 1.8 percent of pre-1949 dwellings between 1999 and 2013 (0.13 percent a year), Berlin demolished nine pre-1919 buildings out of 50,337 in 2022 (0.018 percent), and North Rhine-Westphalia demolished 56 of 445,226 in 2023 (0.013 percent), a pace implying 7,951 years to clear its prewar stock.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: European historic cores are effectively permanent capital — no redevelopment optionality should be priced into central land there.
insights.quote: At this rate, it will take North Rhine-Westphalia 7,951 years to demolish its prewar stock entirely.
insights.locator: In Berlin in 2022, just nine buildings

insights.claim: British government statistics show the number of pre-1919 dwellings actually increasing between 2012 and 2024 because more homes were subdivided than demolished, an outcome that inverts the normal expectation of stock attrition.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: UK marginal housing supply in historic areas comes from subdivision, not replacement — relevant to conversion-led investment strategies.
insights.quote: government statistics show a paradoxical increase in the number of pre-1919 dwellings between 2012 and 2024
insights.locator: In Britain, government statistics show

insights.claim: Modernist planners were in one sense less destructive than their predecessors, because they were halted after demolishing only a substantial minority of the inherited building stock, whereas the Victorians and Georgians continued until they had torn down almost all of it.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: The moral premise underpinning conservation law is empirically shaky, which is the intellectual opening reformers need to attack it.
insights.quote: The idea that postwar planners were moved by destructive animus towards the past is mostly a myth.
insights.locator: The overall picture here is one of striking continuity

insights.claim: Nineteenth-century cities almost never cut railways through their historic cores — producing the ring of termini around central London and Paris — because steam and coal smoke made railways the one form of infrastructure Victorians found overwhelmingly ugly, a natural experiment showing aesthetics could block development even then.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Aesthetic aversion is a durable, predictable veto on specific infrastructure classes — useful for forecasting siting fights over data centers, wind farms and pylons.
insights.quote: nineteenth-century people behaved just like twentieth-century people in respect of the one kind of infrastructure they found overwhelmingly ugly
insights.locator: There is one interesting exception to this destructiveness

insights.claim: Georgians and Victorians treated ordinary buildings as depreciating assets like cars or computers today, assuming that stock degraded with use and that a replacement was probably better, and their leading architectural magazine The Builder claimed in 1868 that private wealth was replacing Georgian street building with a superior Victorian London.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Public belief about whether buildings appreciate or depreciate is the hidden variable governing redevelopment consent — track it, not just zoning text.
insights.quote: normal houses generally declined in value over time, like cars or computers today
insights.locator: On the other hand, many Georgians and Victorians thought

themes.theme: Against the pretext theory of conservation

insights.claim: The theory that heritage conservation is merely a pretext invented by NIMBYs fails on sequencing: suburban zoning was entrenched across Europe before the First World War and across North America between the wars, while conservation only became a serious constraint in the 1960s and 70s, leaving gaps of forty to seventy years that a pretext story cannot explain.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: If conservation is a genuine independent preference rather than a cover story, exposing 'bad faith' will not defeat it — reformers need an aesthetic answer instead.
insights.quote: Why didn’t NIMBYs invent conservationism earlier?
insights.locator: The most obvious problem is once again sequencing

insights.claim: Conservation rules protect working-class housing, commercial downtowns, public buildings, isolated country houses and rural churches far more than they protect the middle-class suburbs NIMBYs actually live in — partly because suburbs were already shielded by zoning — so the movement’s revealed priorities are those of outsiders, not neighbors.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Predicts where heritage risk actually bites: central and commercial sites, not the suburban fringe.
insights.quote: the conservation movement has the priorities of a NITBY movement, not a NIMBY one
insights.locator: The pretextual theory also struggles to explain

insights.claim: The campaign against the Lower Manhattan Expressway, which would have cut through the then-decayed manufacturing and warehouse districts of SoHo and Little Italy, drew support from non-resident grandees including Eleanor Roosevelt, Lewis Mumford, Margaret Mead, Charles Abrams and William H Whyte.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: The canonical American preservation victory was won by outsiders over a low-amenity area — evidence that elite non-local opinion, not resident interest, decides these fights.
insights.locator: Perhaps the most famous of all American conservationist battles

insights.claim: Objections raised at planning committees are frequently pretextual in individual cases — opponents who gutted the historic features of their own homes suddenly champion trivial historic objects, alongside sudden interest in bats, newts, hedgehogs, flood risk and key workers — but individual bad faith cannot explain the origin of the conservation movement as a whole.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Separates case-level obstruction tactics (manageable, priceable) from the structural aesthetic constraint (not manageable by legal drafting).
insights.quote: Intense interest may also be discovered in bats, newts, hedgehogs, bees, blackbirds, public housing tenants, flood risk, key workers, young people, old people, and so on.
insights.locator: When I attend planning committee meetings

themes.theme: The L transect and frozen European cores

insights.claim: Cities with little historic building stock and few central residents develop an ‘L transect’ — a sheer forest of downtown skyscrapers atop vast suburbs petrified at low density — visible in Melbourne’s CBD versus Fitzroy, and also in Miami, Toronto, Calgary and Brisbane.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: A city’s density profile reveals which veto is binding; L-shaped cities offer central high-rise development opportunity but no missing-middle route.
insights.quote: These cities have developed a distinctive ‘L transect’, sheer at the core but flat everywhere else.
insights.locator: Urbanists write about an ‘urban transect’

insights.claim: The building stock of central Paris, Rome and Madrid has hardly changed since 1960, forcing European municipalities to site skyscraper districts on low-end suburban land such as Paris’s La Défense and Madrid’s AZCA, and current plans for towers around the Périphérique could give Paris an inverted ‘U transect’ with peak densities at the periphery.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: European commercial development value migrates to peripheral nodes by regulatory necessity — a structural bid for edge-of-city land.
insights.quote: the building stock of central Paris, Rome, or Madrid has hardly changed at all since 1960
insights.locator: By contrast, European city centers have been more perfectly frozen

insights.claim: Where European centers did densify after 1945 it was generally downstream of heavy bomb damage, as in Frankfurt and London, and one famous study found the Blitz ultimately made London’s economy 10 percent larger by enabling higher densities on former bomb sites.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Quantifies the growth cost of heritage constraint: clearing historic fabric was worth roughly a tenth of London’s economy in agglomeration terms.
insights.quote: One famous study found that the Blitz ultimately made London’s economy 10 percent larger by enabling higher densities on former bomb sites.
insights.locator: Where European cities have densified their centers

insights.claim: If restrictions were purely NIMBY-driven, bombed sites would show lower density today because opposition would have resisted rebuilding from a lower baseline; the fact that they show higher density instead proves heritage protection, not neighbor opposition, is the binding constraint in city centers.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Identifies the actual constraint variable to model when forecasting central-city supply response to planning reform.
insights.quote: The reason that bomb damage enabled higher subsequent densities is that development is often blocked by NITBY protection of heritage architecture, not NIMBY opposition to density.
insights.locator: If London’s development restrictions were solely driven by NIMBYism

insights.claim: Brussels adopted modern development controls unusually late, producing a counterfactual glimpse of a Europe without zoning and heritage restrictions, and the resulting backlash — which put the word ‘Brusselization’ into planning vocabulary — led it to adopt internationally normal restrictions in 1979.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Shows the political half-life of unconstrained central redevelopment: liberalized regimes tend to self-reverse within a generation once uglification is visible.
insights.locator: Brussels adopted modern development controls unusually late

insights.claim: Two mid-century changes made redevelopment read as uglification: traditional styles were superseded by modernism — characterized by lack of ornament, repetitive facade patterns and exposed steel and concrete — and mass car ownership degraded street environments, turning the tree-lined nineteenth-century boulevard into the modern highway that authorities now screen with sight and sound barriers.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Two independent, still-operative forces — style and traffic — must both be reversed for redevelopment to regain default public consent.
insights.quote: This is the main reason that redevelopment switched from being aesthetically neutral to being uglifying.
insights.locator: How did people come to expect that new buildings

insights.claim: Visual preference surveys consistently find that most people prefer traditional architectural styles to modernist ones, making the replacement of prewar traditional buildings with postwar modernist ones a perceived uglification to the general public.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Public taste is measurable and stable — developers who ignore it are buying avoidable political risk on every scheme.
insights.quote: visual preference surveys consistently find that most people prefer traditional styles to modernist ones
insights.locator: It is also true that the dominant architectural styles

insights.claim: Most people are not principled opponents of redevelopment as such — schemes on former industrial or logistics sites like NOMA in Washington DC or Coal Drops Yard in London are often widely popular — which shows that opposition is triggered by perceived uglification rather than by change or density per se.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Brownfield and logistics-site conversion carries structurally lower political risk than historic-core redevelopment — a persistent entitlement-risk arbitrage.
insights.quote: Even today, developments on former industrial or logistics sites are often widely popular, like NOMA in Washington DC or Coal Drops Yard in London.
insights.locator: Most people are not principled opponents of redevelopment

insights.claim: Conservationists have been strikingly ineffective at protecting postwar modernist heritage — England had listed about 300 postwar buildings by 2003, growing to roughly 500 by 2015 out of some 375,000 listed buildings, and the American National Register applies a blanket fifty-year rule — revealing that the movement is driven by beauty rather than age.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Postwar concrete stock is far more redevelopable than prewar stock; heritage risk should be underwritten by architectural style, not merely by building age.
insights.quote: In England, 300 postwar buildings had been listed as of 2003, apparently growing to about 500 in 2015, out of some 375,000 listed buildings in total.
insights.locator: There do exist conservation groups defending modernist architecture

insights.claim: Conservationists were appalled by uglification but avoided direct confrontation with high-status modernism by sublimating their appreciation of beauty into an appreciation of heritage, letting them promote traditional architecture without being accused of pastiche.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: The stated rationale for preservation is not the operative one, so heritage debates conducted on historical-significance grounds will keep missing the real objection.
insights.quote: many conservationists secretly love old buildings because they are beautiful, while pretending to love them because they are old
insights.locator: It also seems to me that the anti-ugliness theory

insights.claim: Within ten or fifteen years of modernism achieving dominance, an immense movement to halt the replacement of old buildings appeared almost from nowhere, after thousands of years in which developers demolished vast quantities of historic stock with barely a whisper of conservationist resistance.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: The tightest empirical link in the essay: architectural taste, not preservation ethics, is the causal trigger for supply-side regulation of central land.
insights.quote: Conservationism was a reaction to postwar redevelopment, as its proponents claimed. But it was less a reaction to what the modernists destroyed, than to what they created.
insights.locator: The anti-ugliness theory of conservationism lines up strikingly

insights.claim: Only about a fifth of housing in the European countries with the oldest stock dates from before 1919, and just 6 percent in the United States, yet the drag on supply far exceeds those shares because historic buildings cluster in city centers and conservation systems also restrict what can be built in the settings and environs of protected buildings.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Headline heritage-share statistics badly understate the constraint — the correct measure is share of high-value central sites encumbered, not share of national stock.
insights.quote: In fact, in most European cities, centers are effectively solid phalanxes of conservation designations, with new development largely displaced to inferior sites on the urban periphery.
insights.locator: How much impact does conservation have on the housing shortage?

insights.claim: Mapping Paris’s pre-1914 buildings shows that, once restrictions on development in the settings of historic buildings are applied, only a handful of sites remain available for development anywhere within the city.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Central Paris supply is effectively fixed; rent and price growth there is a pure demand play with no supply release valve.
insights.locator: Paris with only buildings from before 1914 marked

insights.claim: Manhattan, central Boston and San Francisco lack the blanket conservation designations of Paris, Amsterdam, Madrid or Rome, but large protected areas coincide precisely with where YIMBYs would most like to enable development, making conservation a real if secondary constraint behind suburban zoning.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: US upzoning wins may under-deliver in exactly the highest-value submarkets because a second, separate heritage layer still binds there.
insights.quote: the historic stock that does exist is heavily concentrated in the most economically vital places
insights.locator: The impact of conservation in the United States is smaller

insights.claim: The public feels that the stock of beautiful buildings is finite and irreplaceable, so no economic or transport argument will ever win consent for large-scale demolition of historic fabric — the constraint can only be broken by confidence that change is not disfigurement and will produce cities people can love.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Implies the unlock for central densification is architectural credibility, not cost-benefit analysis — a testable prediction for which reform coalitions succeed.
insights.quote: Their dread of ugliness will hang over our cities like a curse, freezing them in the last moment of their beauty.
insights.locator: For most Westerners today, however
